name: Whipple Disease

criteria.description: Positive PAS (periodic acid-Schiff) staining of foamy macrophages in small intestinal biopsy
Positive Tropheryma whipplei PCR from tissue or body fluid
Clinical features: diarrhea, weight loss, arthralgias, lymphadenopathy
Electron microscopy showing characteristic bacilli in macrophages

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: PAS-positive macrophages in small intestinal biopsy is the classic diagnostic finding. PCR confirmation of T. whipplei is increasingly used. For extraintestinal disease, PCR from affected tissue/fluid.
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Arthralgias may precede GI symptoms by years to decades. Immunocompromised patients may have atypical presentations.

pathognomonic.notes: Steatorrhea and weight loss from fat malabsorption
Often the earliest symptom; may precede GI symptoms by 5-10 years

occasional.notes: Diffuse gray-brown skin darkening, especially sun-exposed areas
Culture-negative endocarditis is a recognized presentation

rare.notes: Pathognomonic for CNS Whipple disease when present; convergent nystagmus with synchronous jaw movements

laboratory: PAS-positive, diastase-resistant macrophages in duodenal biopsies (hallmark)
Anemia (iron and/or folate deficiency from malabsorption)
T. whipplei PCR positive in tissue, stool, saliva, or CSF
imaging: CT abdomen: mesenteric/retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy, often with low-density centers
MRI brain: focal lesions in hypothalamus, periventricular regions in CNS disease
Small bowel imaging may show thickened mucosal folds
genetic: HLA-B27 association reported in some studies
Possible immunogenetic susceptibility involving defective Th1 response
other: Upper endoscopy: pale, shaggy duodenal mucosa with whitish-yellow patches (lymphatic obstruction)
CSF analysis recommended in all cases (PCR for T. whipplei) to assess for CNS involvement
Electron microscopy: rod-shaped bacilli within macrophages

distinguishingFeatures: Celiac has villous atrophy but no PAS-positive macrophages
Differentiated by AFB staining and culture
Sarcoidosis shows non-caseating granulomas, not PAS-positive macrophages

redFlags: Neurological symptoms (oculomasticatory myorhythmia, cognitive changes, seizures) suggesting CNS involvement
Relapse of symptoms during or after treatment (especially neurological relapse)
references: Dolmans RA, et al. Clinical manifestations, treatment, and diagnosis of Tropheryma whipplei infections. Clin Microbiol Rev. 2017;30(2):529-555.
Fenollar F, et al. Whipple's disease. N Engl J Med. 2007;356(1):55-66.
Schneider T, et al. Whipple's disease: new aspects of pathogenesis and treatment. Lancet Infect Dis. 2008;8(3):179-190.
